translation.text:
I asked him again, saying, "Since the Lord has counted me worthy that you should dwell with me always, bear with a few more words from me, since I understand nothing, and my heart has been hardened by my former deeds. Give me understanding, for I am very foolish and altogether perceive nothing."

Answering me, he says, "I," he says, "am over repentance[a][1], and I give understanding to all who repent. Or does it not seem to you," he says, "that this very thing—to repent—is understanding? To repent," he says, "is great understanding. For the man who has sinned[3] understands that he has done what is evil before the Lord, and the deed that he did comes up upon his heart[2], and he repents and no longer works the evil, but works the good lavishly[4], and he humbles his own soul and chastises it, because he sinned. You see then that repentance is great understanding."

"For this reason then," I say, "sir,[5] I seek to learn everything exactly from you: first, because I am a sinner; then, because I do not know by doing what works I shall live, for my sins are many and manifold."

"You will live," he says, "if you keep my commandments and walk in them; and whoever, having heard these commandments, keeps them, will live to God[6]."

footnotes.text: “I am over repentance” can also be rendered “I preside over repentance.” Elsewhere in Mandate 4 the figure is identified as the angel associated with repentance.
Literally “goes up upon his heart,” an idiom for a deed coming forcibly to mind or weighing on one’s conscience.
Some witnesses omit “the man.” The sense is “the one who has sinned.”
“Lavishly” translates πολυτελῶς; alternatives include “abundantly” or “generously.” The term’s core sense is “in costly/splendid fashion.”
Vocative κύριε addressed to the messenger is rendered “sir” here to distinguish from “the Lord” (God) mentioned earlier in the sentence.
“Will live to God” preserves the Greek dative; many would say “live for God.”

Repentance and related expressions are read in this works own context; they are not restricted to feeling sorry, and no uniform Godward formula is imposed. Use repentance for moral change while preserving the works own teaching about baptism, forgiveness, conduct and the angel of repentance; do not impose a different tradition on it.

The only issues are the omission of several repetitive dialogue tags (φησίν/φησί) in verse 2, which are a characteristic feature of Hermas's style, and a minor tense clash in translating the participle ἀποκριθείς.
issues_found: Omission of dialogue tags: The draft omits three instances of φησίν/φησί in verse 2. While repetitive in English, this is a distinct stylistic feature of Hermas's dialogue and should be preserved for author-intent accuracy.

Participle translation: 'He answered me and says' translates the aorist participle ἀποκριθείς as a finite past tense verb, creating an awkward tense clash with the present λέγει. 'Answering me, he says' is smoother and more accurate to the syntax.

Answering me, he says, "I," he says, "am over repentance[a], and I give understanding to all who repent. Or does it not seem to you," he says, "that this very thing—to repent—is understanding? To repent," he says, "is great understanding. footnotes.text: “I am over repentance” can also be rendered “I preside over repentance.” Elsewhere in Mandate 4 the figure is identified as the angel associated with repentance.
Literally “goes up upon his heart,” an idiom for a deed coming forcibly to mind or weighing on one’s conscience.
Some witnesses omit “the man.” The sense is “the one who has sinned.”
“Lavishly” translates πολυτελῶς; alternatives include “abundantly” or “generously.” The term’s core sense is “in costly/splendid fashion.”
Vocative κύριε addressed to the messenger is rendered “sir” here to distinguish from “the Lord” (God) mentioned earlier in the sentence.
“Will live to God” preserves the Greek dative; many would say “live for God.”

Repentance and related expressions are read in this works own context; they are not restricted to feeling sorry, and no uniform Godward formula is imposed. Use repentance for moral change while preserving the works own teaching about baptism, forgiveness, conduct and the angel of repentance; do not impose a different tradition on it.

Keeping the cognate chain transparent strengthens the rhetorical link in the passage that repentance itself is ‘understanding’.

‘Deeds’ fits the moral context and allows ‘works’ later to render ἐργάζομαι without redundancy.
